sub: Named after al-Ḥāqqah, “the Inevitable Reality”, its first word
theme: The Day of Judgement is certain. Nations that denied it were destroyed, every person will be handed their record, and the Quran that warns of it is truly Allah’s word, not a poet’s or a soothsayer’s.
story: One of the earliest surahs revealed in Makkah, when opposition to the Prophet ﷺ had begun but had not yet turned violent. The Quraysh denied the resurrection and dismissed the Prophet ﷺ as a poet or a soothsayer.

Before becoming Muslim, ʿUmar went out to trouble the Prophet ﷺ and found him reciting this surah in prayer. ʿUmar thought, “He must be a poet,” and heard: “not the word of a poet.” Then, “A soothsayer?” And he heard: “nor the word of a soothsayer.”

The surah answers both claims. The first part (1–37) shows the Day: nations destroyed, the world ended, records handed out. The second (38–52) proves the Quran is revelation from the Lord of the worlds. ʿUmar said Islam entered his heart that day, though he accepted it later.

sections.title: The Inevitable Day: Thamūd, ʿĀd, Pharaoh and others destroyed for denying
sections.meaning: Al-Ḥāqqah, the Day that must come, is bigger than you can imagine. Thamūd were destroyed by an overpowering blast, ʿĀd by a freezing wind lasting eight days. Pharaoh and the overturned towns disobeyed their messengers and were seized. When the Flood rose, Allah carried your ancestors in the ship, a lesson for ears that listen.
points: Al-Ḥāqqah! What is al-Ḥāqqah? What will make you know?
Thamūd and ʿĀd denied it; Thamūd destroyed by the overpowering blast
ʿĀd flattened by a raging wind; not one of them left
Pharaoh, those before him, the overturned towns: seized severely
The Flood: your ancestors carried in the ship, a lesson to keep
sections.matters: It makes the surah’s claim, that the Day is real, and backs it with history. Every nation that called it a lie was punished in this world. Their destruction was a small sample of that Day, seen before it arrives.
sections.story: No specific incident. The opening warns the Makkans who denied the resurrection with the fate of earlier nations who denied it.
explained: Al-Ḥāqqah is a name for the Day of Judgement: the reality bound to happen, when every hidden truth comes out. The name is repeated three times to show how huge it is. Thamūd and ʿĀd both denied it. Thamūd were destroyed by aṭ-ṭāghiyah, a blast beyond all limits.

ʿĀd were struck by a freezing, roaring wind for seven nights and eight days without a break, and left lying like hollow palm trunks. Not one survived. Pharaoh, the nations before him and the overturned towns of Lūṭ’s people disobeyed their messengers and were seized. And when the Flood rose, Allah carried your ancestors in the ship.
teaches: Denying the Day doesn’t stop it coming.
Rejecting one messenger means rejecting them all.
Every ship is a reminder of how Allah saved the believers in the Flood.
Be a wāʿiyah ear: listen, understand and keep what you hear.
sections.hook: Al-Ḥāqqah is said three times (1–3). Then the nations in order: Thamūd (5), ʿĀd (6–8), Pharaoh and the overturned towns (9–10), the Flood (11–12). Most ayat rhyme on -iyah: ṭāghiyah, ʿātiyah, khāwiyah, bāqiyah.

sections.title: One Horn blast: earth crushed, sky split, all presented, nothing hidden
sections.meaning: One blast on the Horn. The earth and mountains are lifted and crushed with a single blow. The Event has happened: the sky splits and hangs frail, the angels stand at its edges, and eight carry the Throne. Everyone is presented before Allah, and not one secret stays hidden.
points: One blast on the Horn; earth and mountains crushed in one blow
The Event happens; the sky splits, weak and torn
Angels at its edges; eight carry the Throne above them
You are presented; no secret of yours stays hidden
sections.matters: After the nations destroyed in this world, the surah turns to the destruction still to come. It brings every person to the moment the rest of the surah describes: standing before Allah with nothing hidden.
sections.story: No specific incident. It moves from punishments in this world to the Day of Judgement itself.
explained: The Horn is blown once, because Allah’s command never needs repeating. The earth and the mountains are lifted from their places and crushed flat in a single blow. Then al-Wāqiʿah, the Event, has happened. The sky, so strong before, splits open and hangs weak.

The angels stand along its edges, and eight carry the Throne of your Lord above them. What that looks like is beyond us; we simply believe it. Then everyone is presented to Allah on flat ground with nowhere to hide. No body, no deed and no secret stays hidden.
teaches: Allah’s command doesn’t need repeating: one blast is enough.
Even mountains and the sky will not last.
Nothing is hidden from Allah, even now.
Believe in the unseen as Allah describes it, without guessing how.
sections.hook: Yawmaʾidhin, “that Day”, appears in every ayah from 15 to 18. “One” comes twice before it: nafkhatun wāḥidah (13) and dakkatan wāḥidah (14).

sections.title: Right-hand record: he shows it joyfully, then enjoys a high garden
sections.meaning: Whoever is handed his record in his right hand is overjoyed and calls out: “Here, read my record! I was sure I would meet my account.” He lives a life that pleases him, in a high garden with fruit hanging within reach. “Eat and drink with pleasure for what you sent ahead.”
points: Record in the right hand: “Here, everyone, read my record!”
“I was certain I would meet my account”
A pleasing life in a high garden, fruit close at hand
Eat and drink happily for what you did in days gone by
sections.matters: It shows what believing in the Day actually does. The one who was certain he would face his account prepared for it, and that certainty is what he celebrates. Paradise here is the result of days spent well.
sections.story: Reportedly revealed about Abū Salamah ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, with the left-hand passage (25) about his brother al-Aswad. The meaning covers everyone who receives their record.
explained: People are presented three times; at the third, the records fly into hands. The one who gets his in his right hand is so happy he shows everyone: hāʾumu, “Here, take it and read!” Allah may show a servant his sins, then say: “I covered them for you in the world, and I forgive them today.”

His secret? “I was certain I would meet my account,” so he prepared. Now he lives a life he is pleased with, in a high garden whose fruit hangs low enough to pick standing, sitting or lying down. He is told: “Eat and drink with pleasure, for what you sent ahead in days gone by.”
teaches: Certainty about the Day turns into preparation for it.
The good you send ahead is waiting for you.
Deeds are the means, but entering Paradise is by Allah’s mercy.
Allah may cover a believer’s sins in this world and forgive them on that Day.
sections.hook: Ayat 19–20 end in -iyah words about “my”: kitābiyah, ḥisābiyah. The garden rhymes follow: rāḍiyah, ʿāliyah, dāniyah, khāliyah (21–24). Ayah 25 opens with the same words, but “left”.

sections.title: Left-hand record: chained in Hell for disbelief and neglecting the poor
sections.meaning: Whoever gets his record in his left hand wishes he had never seen it and that death had ended everything. His wealth and power are gone. Seize him, shackle him, burn him, chain him: he never believed in Allah, the Most Great, nor urged feeding the poor. Now he has no friend, no real food.
points: Left hand: if only I’d never seen my record, and death were the end
“My wealth didn’t help me; my power is gone”
Seize him, shackle him, into Hell, into a seventy-cubit chain
He didn’t believe in Allah, the Most Great, nor urge feeding the poor
No friend here, no food but ghislīn, eaten only by sinners
sections.matters: It gives the reason for the punishment in two lines: no faith in Allah, and no care for the poor. Success rests on sincerity to Allah and kindness to His creation, and he had neither. The wealth and power he trusted are the first things to fail him.
sections.story: Reportedly revealed about al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, brother of Abū Salamah. The meaning covers everyone who receives their record in the left hand.
explained: The one handed his record in his left hand cries: “I wish I had never been given it, never known my account! If only death had been the end.” He once hated death more than anything; now he longs for it. “My wealth did not help me. My sulṭān is gone”: his power, or his excuse.

The guardians of Hell are ordered: seize him, collar him, throw him into the Blaze, then bind him in a chain seventy cubits long. Why? He did not believe in Allah, the Most Great, and did not feed the poor or urge others to. So here he has no ḥamīm, no close friend, and no food but ghislīn.
teaches: Wealth and status can’t buy safety on that Day.
Faith in Allah and care for the poor go together.
Even encouraging others to feed the poor matters.
No friend or relative can rescue someone from Allah’s punishment.
sections.hook: Same opening as 19, but bi-shimālihi, “in his left hand”. Four -iyah words of loss: kitābiyah, ḥisābiyah, māliyah, sulṭāniyah. The orders build with thumma: seize and shackle (30), thumma Fire (31), thumma chain (32).

sections.title: An oath by seen and unseen: the Quran isn’t poetry or soothsaying
sections.meaning: Allah swears by everything you see and everything you don’t: this Quran is the word of a noble Messenger, conveyed from Allah. It is not a poet’s words, nor a soothsayer’s. It is revelation sent down from the Lord of the worlds.
points: An oath by what you see and what you don’t see
It is the word of a noble Messenger
Not a poet’s word: how little you believe
Not a soothsayer’s word: how little you reflect
Sent down from the Lord of the worlds
sections.matters: The second half of the surah starts here. The Quraysh called the Prophet ﷺ a poet or a soothsayer to brush off the warning about the Day. These ayat answer both labels, with all creation, seen and unseen, as witness.
sections.story: Before becoming Muslim, ʿUmar heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting this surah. He thought, “A poet,” and heard ayah 41. He thought, “A soothsayer,” and heard ayah 42. He said Islam entered his heart then, though he accepted it later.
explained: Allah swears by what you see and what you do not see: all of creation, or this world and the unseen world. The Quran is the speech of a rasūl karīm, a noble Messenger. He is called a messenger because he only conveys it from the One who sent him.

It is not a poet’s words, as they claimed, nor a kāhin’s, a soothsayer’s. “How little you believe” really means you don’t believe at all. Had they reflected on the Prophet ﷺ and his character, the truth would have been as clear as the sun. It is revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
teaches: The Quran is Allah’s word, not human speech.
Judge a message by the character of the one who brings it.
A heart that truly listens can be changed by a few ayat.
Honest reflection leads to faith.
sections.hook: Qawl, “word”, comes three times: qawlu rasūlin karīm (40), bi-qawli shāʿir (41), bi-qawli kāhin (42). Ayat 41 and 42 both end qalīlan mā: first tuʾminūn, then tadhakkarūn.

sections.title: Had he forged it, Allah would seize him; it is certain truth
sections.meaning: Had the Prophet ﷺ invented anything in Allah’s name, Allah would have seized him by the right hand and cut his heart’s artery, and no one could have stopped it. The Quran is a reminder for the God-conscious, a regret for the deniers, and certain truth. So glorify your Lord, the Most Great.
points: Had he forged sayings in Our name, We’d seize him by the right
Then cut his heart’s artery, and none of you could stop it
A reminder for the righteous; We know some of you deny
A regret for the disbelievers, and the truth of certainty
So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great
sections.matters: It closes the case. The Prophet ﷺ could not add or remove a word, and Allah Himself vouches for what he brings. Then the surah ends not with argument but with worship, telling the Prophet ﷺ to glorify his Lord and not be troubled by them.
sections.story: No specific incident. It answers the claim that the Prophet ﷺ was making the Quran up. When ayah 52 was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ told them to make this glorification part of rukūʿ.
explained: Suppose the Prophet ﷺ had made up even some sayings and put them in Allah’s name. Allah would have seized him by the right hand and cut al-watīn, the artery from the heart, and no one could have shielded him. This is about the Prophet ﷺ; it doesn’t mean every false claimant dies at once.

He never did, so what he brings is true. The Quran reminds those who fear Allah. Some will still deny it, and it will become their ḥasrah, bitter regret, when they see the outcome. It is ḥaqq al-yaqīn: certain truth, with no room for doubt. So glorify your Lord’s name, and don’t let their words distress you.
teaches: The Prophet ﷺ delivered the Quran exactly, adding and removing nothing.
The same Quran is a reminder for some and a regret for others.
When people’s words hurt, turn to glorifying Allah.
The glorification we say in rukūʿ comes from this final ayah.
sections.hook: Four ayat in a row open wa inna: wa innahu (48), wa innā (49), wa innahu (50), wa innahu (51). Al-ʿaẓīm ends ayah 33 and ayah 52. Tadhkirah, “reminder”, appears at 12 and 48.

groups.text: Al-Ḥāqqah, the Day that must come: what is it? Nothing can make you grasp how great it is.
Thamūd and ʿĀd denied the Striking Day. Thamūd were destroyed by an overpowering blast.
ʿĀd were struck by a freezing wind for eight days, left like hollow palm trunks, with no one left.
Pharaoh, those before him and the overturned towns disobeyed their messengers, and Allah seized them severely.
In the Flood, Allah carried your ancestors in the ship, as a reminder for ears that keep what they hear.
One blast on the Horn, and the earth and mountains are lifted and crushed in one blow.
The Event has happened, and the sky splits open, frail and weak.
The angels stand at the sky’s edges, and eight carry the Throne of your Lord above them.
You are presented before Allah, and not one secret stays hidden.
The one given his record in his right hand shows it off: he was certain he would meet his account.
He lives a life he loves, in a high garden with fruit hanging within reach.
“Eat and drink with pleasure for what you sent ahead in the days gone by.”
The one given his record in his left hand wishes he had never seen it, and that death had been the end.
His wealth didn’t help him, and his power is gone.
Seize him, shackle him, throw him into the Blaze, and bind him in a chain seventy cubits long.
He didn’t believe in Allah, the Most Great, nor urge feeding the poor.
Today he has no close friend, and no food but the discharge of wounds, eaten only by sinners.
By all you see and all you don’t, the Quran is the word of a noble Messenger.
It isn’t a poet’s or a soothsayer’s word; it is sent down from the Lord of the worlds.
Had the Prophet ﷺ invented anything in Allah’s name, Allah would have seized him, and no one could have stopped it.
The Quran is a reminder for the God-conscious, a regret for deniers, and the truth of certainty.
So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.

1.explain: Al-Ḥāqqah: a name for the Day of Judgement. It is the reality bound to happen, when every promise and warning comes true and all hidden truths come out.

2.explain: “What is al-Ḥāqqah?” The question doesn’t ask for information. It shows how enormous the Day is.

3.explain: “What will make you know?” You haven’t seen it or its terrors, so it is beyond anything you can picture.

4.explain: Thamūd, the people of Ṣāliḥ, and ʿĀd, the people of Hūd, denied al-Qāriʿah: another name for the Day, because its terrors strike the heart.

5.explain: Aṭ-ṭāghiyah: an overpowering blast, a cry beyond all limits that burst their hearts (or, in another view, their own transgression). Only their bodies and homes were left.

6.explain: Ṣarṣar: a freezing, roaring wind. ʿĀtiyah: violent and beyond all limits, blowing without mercy. The Prophet ﷺ said ʿĀd were destroyed by a westerly wind.

7.explain: Ḥusūm: in unbroken succession, cutting them off completely. For seven nights and eight days they fell dead, like hollow palm trunks knocked to the ground.

8.explain: “Do you see any of them left?” No. Not one survived, and no one even traces his family back to them.

9.explain: Pharaoh came, and those before him (or, in another reading, those with him), and al-muʾtafikāt, the overturned towns of Lūṭ’s people. All brought al-khāṭiʾah: disbelief and sin.

10.explain: Each disobeyed the messenger sent to them. Rābiyah: a seizing beyond the ordinary, severe and destructive. Whoever denies one messenger denies them all.

11.explain: When the water ṭaghā, rose past every limit in Nūḥ’s Flood, Allah carried you, meaning your ancestors, with you in their loins, in al-jāriyah, the sailing ship.

12.explain: “It” is either the ship, since every ship still reminds us, or the whole event: believers saved, deniers drowned. Udhunun wāʿiyah: an ear that hears, understands and keeps.

13.explain: Nafkhatun wāḥidah: a single blast on the Horn, since Allah’s command needs no repeating. It is either the first blast, when all die, or the blast that raises everyone.

14.explain: The earth and mountains are lifted from their places and crushed with one blow, until everything is flat, with no dip or rise.

15.explain: Then al-Wāqiʿah, “the Event”, has happened: another name for the Day of Judgement.

16.explain: The sky splits open. Wāhiyah: once so strong, now frail and torn, shaken by the terror of that Day.

17.explain: Al-malak: the angels, all of them, stand along the sky’s edges. Eight carry the Throne above them: eight angels, or eight ranks of angels. Its true nature is known only to Allah.

18.explain: Tuʿraḍūn: you are presented before Allah. Nothing is hidden: not your bodies, not your deeds, not your secrets. The ground is flat, with nothing to hide behind.

19.explain: Hāʾumu: “Here, all of you, take it and read!” He is so glad he wants everyone to see. People are presented three times; at the third, the records fly into hands.
19.why: Reportedly revealed about Abū Salamah ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbd al-Asad al-Makhzūmī, with the left-hand passage (25) about his brother al-Aswad. The meaning covers everyone given their record in the right hand.

20.explain: Ẓanantu here means “I was certain.” He believed he would meet his account, so he prepared for it. That certainty is what brought him here.

21.explain: ʿĪshatin rāḍiyah: a life he is fully pleased with, holding everything the soul wants, which he would never trade for anything else.

22.explain: In a lofty garden, high in rank and in its homes. Paradise has a hundred levels, each as far apart as the sky is from the earth.

23.explain: Quṭūfuhā dāniyah: its clusters of fruit hang low, within reach whether standing, sitting or lying down.

24.explain: “Eat and drink hanīʾan, with pleasure and nothing to spoil it, for what you sent ahead in the days gone by”: the prayer, fasting, charity and kindness of the world.

25.explain: The same scene, but bi-shimālihi, in his left hand. He cries, “I wish I had never been given my record,” because he knows what is in it.
25.why: Reportedly revealed about al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, brother of Abū Salamah, whose right-hand passage begins at 19. The meaning covers everyone given their record in the left hand.

26.explain: “…and never known what my account is.” He wishes he had been forgotten, never raised and never judged.

27.explain: Al-qāḍiyah: the death that ends everything. He wishes his death in the world had been final, with no life after. The death he hated most, he now longs for.

28.explain: Mā aghnā ʿannī māliyah: “My wealth did not help me.” He sent none of it ahead, and it can’t ransom him now.

29.explain: Sulṭāniyah: his power and position, gone. Or his argument: he has no excuse left. His followers, status and strength have all vanished.

30.explain: The guardians of Hell are told: khudhūhu, seize him, fa-ghullūhu, shackle him, with a collar on his neck and his hands tied to it.

31.explain: Then into al-Jaḥīm, the blazing Fire, with him.

32.explain: Then put him into a chain seventy cubits long, measured by an angel’s arm: either bound in it or threaded on it.

33.explain: The reason: he did not believe in Allah, al-ʿAẓīm, the Most Great. He rejected the messengers and the truth they brought, and gave Allah none of His right.

34.explain: Nor did he urge others to feed the poor, let alone feed them himself. Success rests on faith in Allah and kindness to people, and he had neither.

35.explain: So today he has no ḥamīm here: no relative or close friend to intercede for him or rescue him.

36.explain: No food except ghislīn: the discharge washed from the wounds of the people of the Fire, or, in another view, a tree in Hell.

37.explain: Only al-khāṭiʾūn eat it: the sinners who missed the straight path and took the road to the Fire.

38.explain: Fa-lā uqsimu: “So I swear.” Allah swears by everything you see…

39.explain: …and everything you don’t: all of creation, seen and unseen. Or this world and the Hereafter.

40.explain: The Quran is the word of a rasūl karīm, a noble Messenger: the Prophet ﷺ, who recites it and delivers it from Allah. A messenger only conveys what he is sent with.

41.explain: Not the word of a shāʿir, a poet, as they claimed. Qalīlan mā tuʾminūn, “how little you believe”, really means you don’t believe at all.

42.explain: Nor the word of a kāhin, a soothsayer. “How little you reflect.” Had they reflected on the Prophet ﷺ and his character, the truth would have been as clear as the sun.

43.explain: Tanzīl: sent down from the Lord of the worlds. Speech like this reflects the greatness of the One who spoke it; it could never be a human’s.

44.explain: Taqawwala: to invent words and attribute them to someone. If the Prophet ﷺ had invented any saying in Allah’s name, adding or removing even a little…

45.explain: …Allah would have seized him bil-yamīn: by the right hand, or with power and strength.

46.explain: …then cut al-watīn, the great artery from the heart; once it is cut, death is instant. This is about the Prophet ﷺ, not a rule that every false claimant dies at once.

47.explain: And none of you could have shielded him. So he would never risk lying for your sake. Allah’s support for him is itself proof that he is truthful.

48.explain: Wa innahu la-tadhkirah: the Quran is a reminder for those with taqwā. It reminds them of what benefits their faith and their life, and they act on it.

49.explain: Allah knows that even after all this, some of you will still deny it. It is a warning to them.

50.explain: Ḥasrah: bitter regret. Either the Quran or their denial of it becomes regret for them when they see the believers rewarded and themselves punished.

51.explain: Ḥaqq al-yaqīn: certainty at its highest. There is knowledge you are told (ʿilm al-yaqīn), see (ʿayn al-yaqīn), and experience firsthand (ḥaqq al-yaqīn). The Quran is certain truth, with no doubt in it.

52.explain: Fa-sabbiḥ: declare your Lord free of every flaw, and let that ease the hurt of their words. When it was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ told them to use this glorification in rukūʿ.
